summary: Hugh McNeile Dyer (1832–1875), a commander in the Royal Navy, commanded H.M.S. Torch on the West Coast of Africa in 1871–73. He went out by mail steamer to the Cape and St. Helena, took over the ship, and for about a year cruised from the Congo and Angola to the Gold Coast, Lagos, the Bonny, Fernando Po, and Liberia, going home by Ascension, Dakar, and Gibraltar. The journal was published after his sudden death, with an unsigned introduction by a friend.

He describes surf landings, palavers with chiefs, the transfer of the Dutch forts to Britain, quarrels between neighbouring chiefs, the punishment of river pirates by burning villages, the Kroomen who worked on ships, the Portuguese convicts and slaves in Angola, and fever on board. He writes of Africans with the open contempt of his time and service, and the text uses racial slurs.
